subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Andesitic lava, typical of composite cones at subduction zones, is best described as:
questions.explain: Andesitic magma has intermediate-to-high silica, making it viscous and gas-rich, hence explosive eruptions.

questions.q: S-waves cannot travel through the outer core, which is evidence that the outer core is:
questions.explain: S-waves cannot pass through liquids; their absence beyond the core-mantle boundary indicates a liquid outer core.

questions.q: Which seismic wave type is the fastest and is the first to be recorded at a seismograph?
questions.explain: P-waves are compressional and travel fastest, so they arrive first at a seismometer.

questions.q: The key distinction between earthquake magnitude and intensity is that magnitude measures:
options: The energy released at the source, while intensity measures felt/observed effects
The felt and observed effects at the surface
The depth of the focus only
questions.explain: Magnitude (e.g. moment magnitude) quantifies energy released at the source, whereas intensity (e.g. Mercalli) describes the shaking felt and damage observed.

questions.q: A nuee ardente (pyroclastic flow), as at Montserrat, is a secondary volcanic hazard consisting of:
options: A fast, hot mixture of gas, ash and rock fragments flowing downslope
questions.explain: Pyroclastic flows are superheated, ground-hugging avalanches of gas, ash and volcanic debris that move at lethal speed.

questions.q: On a Park model curve, a country with strong management and resources would be expected to show:
options: A shallower dip and faster return to (or above) the pre-disaster level
A deeper drop and slower recovery
questions.explain: Greater capacity to cope reduces the depth of the decline and speeds rehabilitation and reconstruction.

questions.q: Which margin type is associated with the deepest-focus earthquakes and explosive andesitic volcanoes?
questions.explain: Subduction at an oceanic-continental destructive margin produces a Benioff zone of deep earthquakes and explosive andesitic stratovolcanoes.

questions.q: Palaeomagnetism provided key evidence for sea-floor spreading because it revealed:
options: A uniform magnetic field across all ocean floor
Symmetrical magnetic stripes of alternating polarity either side of mid-ocean ridges
questions.explain: As basalt cools it locks in Earth's magnetic polarity, producing symmetrical stripes of normal and reversed polarity that mirror across a ridge.

questions.q: The moment magnitude scale (Mw) is logarithmic; an increase of one whole unit represents roughly how much more energy released?
questions.explain: Each whole step on the magnitude scale corresponds to about a 32-fold increase in energy released.

questions.q: Liquefaction during an earthquake occurs when:
options: Saturated, loose sediment temporarily behaves as a fluid under shaking
questions.explain: Ground shaking raises pore-water pressure in saturated unconsolidated sediment so it loses strength and behaves like a liquid.

questions.q: Why do similar-magnitude earthquakes often cause far fewer deaths in high-income than low-income countries?
options: Magnitude is always lower in rich countries
Greater capacity: enforced building codes, monitoring, planning and emergency services
questions.explain: Higher development brings resilient construction, early-warning systems and effective emergency response, reducing vulnerability.

questions.q: Higher silica content in magma tends to make eruptions more explosive because it:
options: Lowers viscosity and allows gas to escape easily
Increases viscosity, trapping gases until pressure is released violently
questions.explain: Silica-rich (felsic/andesitic) magma is viscous, so dissolved gases cannot escape easily and build pressure for explosive eruptions.

questions.q: As a tsunami approaches shallow coastal water it:
options: Decreases in height and increases in speed
Slows down and increases dramatically in height (shoaling)
questions.explain: In shallow water the wave slows and its energy is compressed, causing wave height to build greatly through shoaling.

questions.q: Basaltic (mafic) lava typically produces which volcano type?
questions.explain: Low-silica basaltic lava is runny and flows far, building broad, gently-sloping shield volcanoes.

questions.q: A lahar is a volcanic hazard formed when:
options: Magma rises through a hot spot
Volcanic ash and debris mix with water to form a fast-moving mudflow
questions.explain: Lahars are mudflows of volcanic ash and debris mobilised by rain or melting ice, often very destructive.

questions.q: Resilience to tectonic hazards is best described as the ability of a community to:
options: Absorb, adapt to and recover from a hazard event
Predict the exact time of every earthquake
questions.explain: Resilience is the capacity to withstand, adapt to and bounce back from a hazard impact.

questions.q: Multiple-hazard zones (e.g. the Philippines) experience compounded risk because they:
options: Are exposed to several physical hazards plus high vulnerability
Lie far from any plate boundary
questions.explain: Such regions face overlapping tectonic and climatic hazards combined with social and economic vulnerability.

questions.q: Mantle convection currents are driven primarily by:
options: Heat from radioactive decay in the core and mantle
questions.explain: Heat from radioactive decay (and residual primordial heat) sets up convection cells in the mantle.

questions.q: At a collision (continental-continental) margin such as the Himalayas, there is generally:
options: Crustal thickening and fold mountains with no subduction
questions.explain: Two continental plates of similar density collide, buckling and thickening the crust into fold mountains without significant subduction.

questions.q: At a constructive (divergent) oceanic plate margin, the characteristic landform and process is:
options: Deep ocean trench and explosive volcanism
Mid-ocean ridge with effusive basaltic eruptions
questions.explain: Diverging plates allow basaltic magma to rise, creating mid-ocean ridges with gentle effusive eruptions.

questions.q: The point within the Earth where an earthquake originates is the:
questions.explain: The focus (hypocentre) is the underground point of rupture; the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.

questions.q: Ridge push (gravitational sliding) operates because newly formed oceanic lithosphere at a mid-ocean ridge is:
options: Denser and colder than older lithosphere
Elevated and slides down the sloping asthenosphere away from the ridge
questions.explain: At ridges the hot, raised lithosphere slides down the flanks under gravity, pushing the plate away from the ridge axis.

questions.q: Conservative (transform) margins produce earthquakes but no volcanoes because:
options: Plates slide past one another, so no crust is created or destroyed
Plates move apart, allowing magma up
Magma is too viscous to erupt
questions.explain: At conservative margins plates move laterally past each other; crust is neither created nor subducted, so there is friction-driven seismicity but no magma generation.

questions.q: Hot spots such as Hawaii are explained by:
options: A plume of rising magma from the mantle independent of plate boundaries
questions.explain: A stationary mantle plume melts the overriding plate as it moves, producing a chain of volcanoes away from any margin.

questions.q: Tsunamis are most commonly generated by:
options: Vertical displacement of the sea floor during a submarine earthquake
questions.explain: Sudden vertical movement of the sea floor, typically at subduction zones, displaces the water column and generates a tsunami.

questions.q: The greatest damage to surface structures in an earthquake is usually caused by:
questions.explain: Slower surface waves have large amplitudes and cause the strongest ground shaking and structural damage.

questions.q: In the disaster-risk (risk = hazard x vulnerability / capacity) equation, risk is reduced by:
questions.explain: Because capacity to cope is the denominator, raising it lowers overall disaster risk.

questions.q: In the Park (hazard-response) model, the curve plots quality of life or economic activity against:
options: Time, through pre-disaster, disruption, relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction phases
questions.explain: Park's model shows quality of life over time across stages from relief through rehabilitation to reconstruction.

questions.q: Effective hazard governance to build resilience typically integrates:
options: Mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery across scales and stakeholders
questions.explain: Good governance combines prediction, prevention, preparedness and recovery, engaging governments, NGOs and communities.

questions.q: Which force, generated by the sinking of a dense, cold oceanic plate at a subduction zone, is now regarded as the dominant driver of plate motion?
questions.explain: Slab pull arises as a cold, dense subducting slab sinks into the mantle and is considered the most significant force moving plates.
